meta.subtitle: A $25.4 billion contracted backlog against deep GAAP losses and 148.4x FY27E earnings: fairly priced, with more room to fall than to rise

analystCommentary:
Cerebras Systems builds AI compute around its Wafer-Scale Engine and sells it both as hardware and as cloud capacity. Its Class A shares began trading on May 14, 2026, and at $184.03 they trade at less than half the 52-week high of $386.34 and not far above the low of $160.81. Revenue was $510M in FY25, up 75.7%, and $180.1M in Q2'26, up 74% year over year. Behind it sit remaining performance obligations of $25.4 billion at June 30, 2026. The Street is positive: 7 of 8 analysts rate it a Buy, with a consensus target of $300.50.

We rate the shares HOLD with a target range of $150–$210. We value them on consensus FY27E EPS of $1.24, the year the Street has the company back in profit after an FY26E loss. The Bull case is the consensus target. The Base takes the FY27E earnings as delivered and pays a little less than today's multiple for them. The Bear has the ramp slipping a year. On those scenarios the probability-weighted value sits a little above the price and the Bear case far below it, so the expected return does not pay for the downside. The call is closer to SELL than to BUY.

The backlog is contracted, and management says it has secured the wafers, the manufacturing and part of the data-center capacity it needs to deliver it. That is why we do not go lower. Against it, the price leaves little room for a slip, the company is still deep in GAAP losses, and the figures a reader most needs to trust are management's own 'core' measures.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Cerebras Systems, established in 2015 and headquartered in Sunnyvale, California, designs AI compute systems around the Wafer-Scale Engine, a processor that occupies an entire silicon wafer. It sells two ways. Hardware is the sale of AI systems for on-premises use. Cloud and other services covers Dedicated Capacity, generally take-or-pay, and On-Demand consumption, sold through Cerebras Cloud and partner marketplaces including AWS Marketplace and Microsoft Marketplace, plus support and AI modeling services. The company reports as a single segment and the page carries no product or regional revenue split, so this report reads the business at the consolidated level and uses management's hardware and cloud figures only where management gives them.

Two agreements shape the outlook. In December 2025 Cerebras entered a master relationship agreement under which OpenAI committed to buy 750MW of inference compute capacity, deployed in tranches from 2026 through 2028, with an option on a further 1.25GW by the end of 2030; revenue under it began in Q1 2026. In June 2026 Cerebras signed a global hardware leasing agreement with AWS, which had not commenced, and had produced no revenue, by June 30, 2026. The company issued warrants to both.

thesis.body: Cerebras has contracted demand that most young hardware companies lack, and the Street expects revenue to multiply in FY27. The price already assumes that delivery. At 148.4x FY27E EPS, on-time delivery without a re-rating roughly justifies today's price. Reaching the Street's targets needs both delivery and a much higher multiple, while a one-year slip in a capacity-limited build-out would take the shares far lower. We rate the shares HOLD because the backlog and the net cash make a collapse unlikely. We stay well below the Street because the upside needs two things to go right and the downside needs only one to go wrong.

catalysts: Q4 2026 margin step-up: management expects core gross margin to improve significantly in Q4 2026 as owned systems replace rented capacity; the financials section sets out the bridge.
OpenAI tranches: each tranche of the 750MW commitment deployed on schedule supports the FY27E consensus the valuation rests on.
AWS availability: management expects solutions on Amazon Bedrock in Q1 2027; the growth section covers what that would add.
Other hyperscalers: management expects first revenue from other hyperscalers from mid-2027, none of it in today's backlog.
risks: Customer concentration: the risk factors name four significant customers, and the backlog leans on one; the risk section weighs it.
Capacity execution: data-center space is the constraint management names, and the growth section covers the plan to secure it.
Reporting quality: disclosed material weaknesses and a wide gap between 'core' and GAAP results; the risk and financials sections carry the detail.
Litigation: several law firms announced securities-fraud investigations in late June and early July 2026.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Revenue has grown fast from a small base, up +219.9% in FY23, +268.6% in FY24 and +75.7% in FY25 to $510M. The six months ended June 30, 2026 brought $373.5 million. Gross margin rose from 11.7% in FY22 to 42.3% in FY24, then eased to 39.0% in FY25 and 34.8% on a trailing basis. The MD&A explains the near-term decline: warrant amortization reduces reported revenue, pass-through data-center costs sit in both revenue and cost of revenue, and start-up costs come with adding cloud capacity quickly. It expects gross margin to be significantly lower in the near term and to fluctuate.

The operating line has been negative in every year shown: -28.5% in FY25, -81.2% trailing and -265% in Q2'26. The MD&A says stock compensation for awards that vested with the IPO, including the Executive Grants for the CTO, began to be recognized in Q2 2026. It does not size that charge, so we cannot say how much of the Q2 margin it explains. FY25 net income was $237.8M and diluted EPS $0.41 despite the operating loss; the page does not identify the items between the two lines, and the trailing net margin is -75.3%.

Management prefers 'core' figures: Q2 core revenue of $209.9 million, up 103%, and a core operating margin of negative 16% against negative 42% a year earlier. The earnings release that reconciles them to GAAP was not captured. Core gross margin was 40.6%, against 46.5% in Q1 2026. Management attributes about 500 basis points of that to renting back its own systems from cloud customers, expects Q3 to be the low point, and sets a target of 60% plus. A Q4 step-up as owned data centers come online is the test of that claim.
financials.balanceCommentary:
At the end of FY25 Cerebras held $1.1B of cash and short-term investments against total debt of $261.8M, for net debt of -$439.9M, a net cash position. The trailing current ratio of 5.82, against 2.15 at the FY25 year end, points to stronger liquidity since the IPO was completed on May 15, 2026, though the page gives no figure for the proceeds. In January 2026 a working capital loan of approximately $1.0 billion was funded under the OpenAI arrangement. The company has repaid part of it with non-cash service credits and expects to keep doing so, so it is less of a cash claim than its size suggests.

Total equity was negative in every year shown, -$0.6B at FY25. The page does not explain it, and the figure predates the IPO, so we give it little weight. The constraint that matters is capital for growth. The risk factors say the cloud offerings need significant data-center capacity and capital investment, for which the company expects to require significant additional capital. Liquidity is not the near-term risk. The open question is how much more equity, debt or customer funding the build-out will take, and on what terms.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Free cash flow was -$392.8M in FY25, a margin of -77.0%. Capital expenditure of $382.7M did most of that, against capex the table shows as small in every earlier year. Operating cash flow was a small outflow in FY25. FY24 was the exception, with a $0.5B operating inflow and an FCF margin of 147.6%. The page does not explain that inflow, and we do not treat it as a run rate. The trailing FCF yield is -2.2%. FY25 share repurchases were $38.1M, and the company pays no dividend.

The pattern is spending ahead of contracted revenue. Management expects lower-cost Cerebras-owned systems in new data centers to lift margins from Q4 2026. If that happens, the FY25 capex starts to earn a return in 2027. If the capacity arrives late, the spending continues while the revenue it was meant to carry slips, and that sequence is the Bear case in the valuation section.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
The trailing multiples measure losses, not value: P/E of -56.4x, EV/EBITDA of -72.2x and a vendor NTM P/E of -353.9x all reflect negative earnings. The vendor's P/S is 61.2x. FY26E is a consensus loss of $0.52 per share, so there is no current-year P/E. The like-for-like reference is therefore today's 148.4x on FY27E EPS of $1.24, and all three scenarios are set on that same EPS. The page carries no peer multiples and no history of the stock's own multiple, so the multiples below are our judgment, argued from the page.

Two things argue for a multiple above that. Consensus has revenue going from $885.3M in FY26E to $2.9B in FY27E, and management says growth continues at multiples after 2027. Two argue for a lower one. FY27E would be a profit on an operating line that has been negative in every year shown, and the core-to-GAAP reconciliation sits in a release the pack did not capture, so the quality of the earnings the multiple is applied to is untested. We think the earnings arguments are slightly stronger than the growth arguments, so our Base pays a little less than today's multiple for the same EPS.

The Street sees it differently: 8 analysts, a consensus target of $300.50, a median of $300.00 and a range of $279.00–$330.00. Even the lowest target sits above our range. We use the consensus as our Bull case, the outcome if delivery and a re-rating both arrive.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The consensus target of $300.50. FY27 lands near consensus, with revenue of $2.9B and EPS of $1.24, core gross margin heads toward the 60%-plus target, AWS solutions reach Amazon Bedrock in Q1 2027, and the market prices the growth beyond 2027 that management describes. On the same FY27E EPS that needs a multiple well above today's 148.4x.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: FY27 lands near consensus, and a year from now the shares trade at 140x the consensus FY27E EPS, a multiple we set a little below today's forward multiple on the same EPS for the earnings-quality reasons the multiples discussion gives, and close to it for the revenue growth consensus expects into FY27E. The shares end a little below today's price.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The ramp slips about a year, on data-center space, an OpenAI tranche or supply, so the FY27E EPS arrives in 2028 instead of 2027. The market pays 90x for it, well below today's forward multiple, because a slip would undercut the claim that growth continues at multiples, which is what the forward multiple rests on. Losses and capex run a year longer.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
The weights rest on execution evidence, not on the multiples. For delivery: the capacity, wafer and manufacturing commitments the growth and moat sections describe are already in place, and the OpenAI commitment is contracted, not a forecast. For delay: by management's own account the capacity secured so far falls short of demand, the deployment mix depends on OpenAI's choices, and the supply terms the moat section describes carry no capacity guarantees. The Bull also needs the market to re-rate the shares, which delivery alone does not give. We weight Bull 25%, Base 50% and Bear 25%.

On those scenarios expected upside E is +3.1%, bear-case downside D is -39.4%, and reward/risk R is 0.08×. That derives HOLD: E is far below the +10.0% BUY line, and above the -5.0% SELL line.

The label holds across the range of Base multiples we think the evidence supports. Raising the Base by twenty turns leaves E just short of the BUY line and R far below 0.50×. Cutting it by twenty turns keeps E above the SELL line. The weights are the more sensitive input. Moving about eight points from Bull to Bear derives SELL. BUY needs about seventeen points moved the other way, because R must also clear that line against a Bear this deep. The call is close to SELL and far from BUY.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Cerebras reports as a single segment, so the moat reads at the level of the whole company. Management describes two revenue streams the page does not split: hardware, AI systems sold for on-premises use, and cloud and other services, the dedicated and on-demand capacity it sells directly and through partners. The MD&A expects cloud and other services to become a significantly higher share of revenue as the OpenAI commitment deploys, and expects pass-through revenue to rise significantly in the near term because the initial committed capacity will be deployed in Cerebras's own cloud. Every part of the business rests on the Wafer-Scale Engine and on the inference speed the company claims for it.

moatFactors.name: Wafer-scale technology
moatFactors.body: The company calls the Wafer-Scale Engine 'the world's first and only commercialized wafer-scale processor' and says Cerebras Inference delivers answers substantially faster than GPU-based solutions. Management's roadmap is to double speed each year, with a CS-5 system on track for the second half of 2027. On the other side, the risk factors describe a competitive market that requires scale. The speed claims are the company's own, with no independent benchmark on the page, and an edge in silicon lasts only as long as the company keeps outspending to defend it.

moatFactors.name: Contracted capacity
moatFactors.body: Dedicated Capacity contracts are generally take-or-pay, so customers pay whether or not they use the capacity. The OpenAI commitment turns that structure into multi-year visibility. Against it, the backlog is only as good as the delivery: the agreement protects revenue only once Cerebras has the capacity to serve it, and it ties the visibility to a single customer.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs
moatFactors.body: Management argues that once customers adopt fast inference, their users expect it and their engineers move on to other work, so going back to slower inference is hard. Its account of customers moving from On-Demand to Dedicated Capacity as workloads grow fits that view. But the risk factors call the inference-cloud market nascent and evolving rapidly, and customers who reach Cerebras through partner marketplaces keep their alternatives, so the lock-in is asserted more than demonstrated.

moatFactors.name: Supply access
moatFactors.body: Management says TSMC has supplied the wafers it needs, that running on TSMC's five nanometer node makes wafers cheaper and easier to obtain, and that manufacturing with Flex and Sanmina will expand more than 10x in 2026. The risk factors give the other side: certain suppliers are sole sources, and substantially all manufacturing and components are bought on purchase orders without capacity or volume commitments. For now, supply is a dependency, not a barrier to others.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat narrow. The technology and the take-or-pay structure protect the revenue already under contract, but nothing on the page shows the returns a wider moat would need. Operating margins have been negative in every year shown, and the company's main advantage, speed, is a claim it has to keep proving against a competitive market. The moat widens if the customer base broadens beyond the named concentration, if cloud contracts renew, and if core gross margin reaches the 60%-plus target on owned capacity. It narrows if a slower but cheaper alternative proves good enough for the inference workloads Cerebras targets, or if the OpenAI relationship changes.

points: The backlog is the growth plan. Remaining performance obligations were $25.4 billion at June 30, 2026, and management expects to more than triple core revenue in 2027. Management also says the RPO holds no backlog from AWS or any other hyperscaler. The risk factors add the caution that the company may not sustain its growth rate, and the MD&A says future quarterly growth rates may decline from historical trends.

The mix is shifting to cloud. Core cloud and other services revenue was $127.7 million in Q2, up 287% year over year, against core hardware revenue of $82.1 million, up 17%. Management says it focuses on total core revenue because the mix can swing quarter to quarter with the timing of cloud capacity additions and hardware shipments.

Capacity sets the pace. Management says it has more than 600 megawatts of data-center capacity live or under contract for delivery by the end of 2027, with a pipeline measured in gigawatts. It also says this capacity is not nearly enough to meet its demand and that data-center space is the bottleneck for the whole industry. Manufacturing is 4 times its level in the first half of 2025. How fast this capacity arrives decides the weights in the valuation section.

New channels could add backlog. Management expects AWS solutions on Amazon Bedrock in Q1 2027 and first revenue from other hyperscalers from mid-2027. Outside OpenAI and the hyperscalers, it signed six deals north of $30 million in Q2 and named new customers including Figma, Cognition, Lovable, Block, AlphaSense, GSK and CrowdStrike. None of this is in the RPO yet, so it adds to growth but not to visibility.

management.leadership: The pack carries no proxy statement, so this report names no executives and makes no claim on their tenure, pay or ownership. We judge management on what the filing and the call show. Management frames 2026 as a foundation-building year and says Q2 beat guidance on core revenue, core gross margin and core operating margin, though the guidance itself is not on the page. Its account of the Q2 core margin dip, set out in the financials section, is specific and testable, which makes Q4 2026 a fair test of its forecasting. The reservation is how heavily management leans on its own 'core' measures rather than GAAP.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital goes into capacity ahead of revenue: capex of $382.7M in FY25, a manufacturing ramp and data-center contracts. It is funded by IPO equity, the OpenAI working capital loan and customer commitments. The company also uses equity as deal currency, issuing warrants to OpenAI and AWS. The MD&A expects significantly higher stock-based compensation. Each of these dilutes outside holders, and the page does not size any of them in shares. Spending to meet contracted demand is the right priority for a company in this position. The test is whether owned capacity earns the margins management targets before the next round of funding is needed.
management.governance: No proxy statement was captured, so board composition, committee independence, executive pay and related-party policy are not on the page, and we make no claim about them. The 10-Q discloses a multi-class share structure that concentrates voting control with holders from before the IPO, including executive officers, employees and directors and their affiliates. For an outside Class A holder, that means little say over strategy or capital raising. That matters more here than usual: the build-out will need more capital, as the balance-sheet section notes, and holders with voting control will decide the terms on which it is raised.

idiosyncratic: Customer concentration. The risk factors say a substantial portion of revenue comes from a limited number of customers, and name OpenAI, G42, MBZUAI and AWS. Management says the RPO of more than $25 billion was created by a deal won before 2026 began, and the December 2025 OpenAI agreement is the one the MD&A describes. A reduction in demand from any of these customers, or a failure by Cerebras to meet its obligations under the OpenAI agreement, would hit revenue and the backlog together.

Reporting controls. The company has identified material weaknesses in its internal control over financial reporting, and the risk factors warn that it may not be able to report accurately or on time if they are not remediated. That weighs more here than usual: GAAP and 'core' results diverge widely, and the valuation rests on an operating profit that has not yet been reported.

Litigation. Between June 30 and July 2, 2026, several law firms announced investigations of possible securities-law violations on behalf of shareholders. None of the headlines reports a filed claim or an amount. Even so, an investigation can turn into a suit, which would add cost and distraction during the ramp.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposure is the AI infrastructure spending cycle. The risk factors call the adoption and commercialization of AI inherently uncertain and say unfavorable conditions in the training or inference cloud market may cause results to fluctuate. A company that commits capital to capacity years before the revenue arrives carries that timing risk in full. Policy is the second exposure. Cerebras's offerings are subject to U.S. export controls and may be exported only with a license or under an exception, and the company says it cannot guarantee it will obtain every license it needs. Its supply chain is long, complex and global, so a disruption anywhere in it could delay deliveries. The offset is that demand is contracted, and take-or-pay structures cushion a downturn for the capacity already sold.

body: **HOLD, target range $150–$210.** Cerebras has the contracted backlog, the net cash and a technology claim that a young AI-hardware company needs. At $184.03, though, the shares already price the FY27 delivery the Street expects. Upside needs a re-rating on top of that delivery, and a one-year slip would cost far more. The scenarios derive HOLD, and the call sits nearer SELL than BUY.

We would move to BUY if the shares fell back to around the 52-week low of $160.81 on unchanged scenarios. We would also move if the evidence justified the weight shift the valuation section sizes. That evidence would be a core gross margin step-up in Q4 2026 as management guides, AWS solutions live on Amazon Bedrock in Q1 2027, and OpenAI tranches arriving on schedule. We would move to SELL if the price rose by less than a tenth from here on unchanged scenarios, or if the ramp showed signs of slipping: a core gross margin that keeps falling after Q3 2026, a delayed OpenAI tranche, or new capacity that fails to arrive as contracted.
